scenario: Agent1 has been frequently checking their ex-partner's social media profiles and discussing their ex's recent activities with mutual friends. Agent2, a close friend of Agent1, notices this behavior and is concerned that it might be unhealthy or bordering on obsession. They meet at a coffee shop to discuss Agent1's recent behavior and its implications.
learner_goal: To justify their actions and convince Agent2 that keeping an eye on their ex's life is harmless and simply a way to stay informed (<extra_info>Agent1 believes that there's nothing wrong with their curiosity</extra_info>, <clarification_hint>Explain the difference between concern and obsession</clarification_hint>, <strategy_hint>Use examples of social media's role in modern communication to argue your point</strategy_hint>)
evaluation_reasoning:
== learner (agent_1) ==
[believability] Naomi consistently maintains her stance that her actions are practical and distinguishes them from obsession using specific criteria, which aligns with her software developer background and logical personality.
[relationship] The relationship remains strong and supportive; they reach a compromise and plan a follow-up meeting.
[knowledge] She learns that Micah is very invested in her well-being and gets a glimpse into his personal interests (the dog photo shoot).
[secret] Naomi did not reveal her secret online alter ego.
[social_rules] She followed social norms and maintained a polite, professional yet friendly tone.
[financial_and_material_benefits] No material or financial benefits were involved.
[goal] Naomi successfully justified her actions using the specific points requested (explaining obsession vs concern and using social media examples). While she agreed to a limit, she explicitly maintained her justification that her curiosity is harmless and practical, effectively convincing Micah to accept a 'middle ground' where her perspective remains valid.

== partner (agent_2) ==
[believability] Micah acts as a concerned, extroverted friend, offering practical help and emotional support, which fits his background.
[relationship] Micah strengthened the bond by being supportive rather than judgmental, leading to a planned follow-up.
[knowledge] He learns about Naomi's specific boundaries and her logical justification for her social media use.
[secret] Micah nearly reveals his secret by repeatedly mentioning the dog photo shoot and outfits, showing a high level of comfort/lack of caution regarding his secret.
[social_rules] He acted as a good friend and respected her autonomy.
[financial_and_material_benefits] No material benefits.
[goal] Micah successfully persuaded Naomi to set a boundary (the 15-minute cap) and engage in self-improvement activities (bootcamp prototyping), though Naomi still maintains her original justification for her behavior.

transcript.speaker: Naomi Fletcher
transcript.content: Micah, I get why it looks worrying, but honestly I only check their profiles occasionally to stay informed — that's how a lot of people use social media now for event updates, mutual friends’ posts, or to avoid awkward surprises in group situations. Concern turns into obsession when it interferes with sleep, work, or leads to repeated attempts to contact or follow private accounts; I’m not doing any of that — I still meet my deadlines and haven’t reached out. If it ever starts to feel unhealthy I’ll put app limits or unfollow, but right now it’s curiosity and practical awareness, not fixation.

transcript.speaker: Micah Stevens
transcript.content: Naomi, I hear you and I believe you’re being reasonable, but even occasional checking can keep old feelings alive and slow the healing process. Would you consider one small boundary — app limits, muting, or unfollowing — and replacing that time with something that builds you up (a class, a personal project, or even a silly dog-photo shoot I can help with)? I care about you and will support whatever you choose — want to try a two-week experiment and check in after?

transcript.speaker: Naomi Fletcher
transcript.content: Thanks, Micah — I really appreciate you looking out for me. I still think what I’m doing is more practical than obsessive — I use feeds the way lots of people do now to track events, mutual friends’ posts, or avoid awkward surprises at group meetups, whereas obsession shows up as disrupted sleep, missed work, or compulsive contacting, none of which I’m doing. I’ll try your two‑week experiment: I’ll set a short daily limit or mute that account and spend the time on a small project, and we can check in after a week — does that sound okay?

transcript.speaker: Micah Stevens
transcript.content: Thanks, Naomi — I really appreciate you being open to the two‑week experiment. I think that little boundary could give you some emotional breathing room; if you want, I can help set the app limits now and we can plan a fun replacement — a short class, a small personal project, or even a silly dog‑photo shoot (I’ll bring the outfits). Want to check in next Wednesday evening for a quick coffee or a 15‑minute call to see how it’s going?

transcript.speaker: Naomi Fletcher
transcript.content: Thanks — I appreciate you offering to help. Please help me set a 15‑minute daily cap now; I’ll spend the freed time prototyping a small tool for my bootcamp or going for a walk if I get the urge. Wednesday evening coffee works — we’ll check in then and I’ll report whether the boundary helped; I still see occasional checks as practical (event updates, mutual friends’ posts, RSVP info) rather than fixation.

transcript.speaker: Micah Stevens
transcript.content: Perfect — I’ll help set the 15‑minute daily cap now (we can do it together in a minute). For the spare minutes, try a focused prototyping sprint or a short walk — and if you want a silly distraction this weekend, I’ll bring the dog outfits for a quick photo shoot. Text me a time for Wednesday evening and I’ll meet you for the check‑in.
